**Orientation**

Van Gogh's iconic Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear rewards two positions. Start a step or two back, roughly centred, so the whole room behind him comes into view: an open window on one side, an easel, and a Japanese print on the wall. From a distance these read as one interior. Then move in close and stand slightly to one side, so the gallery light rakes across the surface. From that angle the paint stops being flat colour and becomes ridges. These raised marks are what Van Gogh wanted you to see, and from straight on they almost disappear.

**The Work**

Van Gogh shows himself in a green overcoat and a blue cap trimmed with black fur. A white bandage covers one ear and wraps down under his chin. The cap was a recent purchase. He bought it to hold the heavy dressing in place and to keep out the winter cold, so even his clothing records the injury.

The bandage appears over his right ear, but it was his left ear he had cut. He painted the portrait by looking into a mirror, which reversed the image. What you see is his reflection, not the face others saw.

title: Georges Seurat
output:
# Georges Seurat: *Young Woman Powdering Herself*

## Orientation

Seurat's *Young Woman Powdering Herself* is best seen from two distances. From a few paces back, the wall behind the woman looks like a smooth field of shifting light and shade. Step closer and that field breaks apart into thousands of small, separate dots of colour, which is how Seurat built the whole image. Then look to the top left-hand corner, at the vase of flowers. That patch hides the most personal secret in the painting.

## The Work

A young woman sits at a small dressing table, powder puff raised, absorbed in her own reflection. The painting dates from between 1888 and 1890, and it is one of the major works Seurat completed before his early death.

The technique matters most here. Seurat did not mix his colours on the palette. He placed small dots of pure, unmixed colour side by side and varied how densely and intensely he clustered them. The modulation of light and shadow on the wall comes entirely from those changing concentrations. Where the dots crowd together or deepen in tone, the wall darkens. Where they thin out or brighten, it seems to glow. Your eye does the blending, so the colour stays vivid rather than muddy.

This method is called pointillism, after the French word for a point or dot. Seurat developed it together with the painter Paul Signac. It became the signature of Neo-Impressionism, the movement that took the Impressionists' interest in light and tried to make it systematic and almost scientific.

The subject is intimate. The model was Madeleine Knobloch, Seurat's mistress, who bore him two sons. Seurat kept this relationship largely private, so the painting is unusually personal: a portrait of the woman he shared his life with, caught in a private daily ritual.

# Springtime (1872): Audio Description

## Orientation

Stand a few steps back from **Springtime (1872)**, roughly in the centre of the gallery floor rather than right up against the frame. Up close, the canvas breaks apart into separate touches of paint. From a little distance, those touches settle into what Monet was chasing: sunlight filtering through a canopy of lilacs and landing in bright patches on the ground and across a woman's pale muslin dress. Then move closer to her face, which Monet painted in sharper focus than anything around it.

## The Work

A young woman sits quietly reading in a garden, shaded by flowering lilacs. She is Camille Doncieux, Monet's first wife. The painting has gone by two names. Today it is called *Springtime*, and it is also known as *The Reader*.

The key to the picture is light. Monet did not paint the sun directly. He showed it breaking through leaves and scattering across the scene, so that the muslin of Camille's dress catches it in irregular pools. That fine, thin cotton fabric becomes a surface for recording light, and the dappled patches are the real subject as much as the woman herself. Her face and figure are held in close focus, which gives her a calm stillness at the centre of all that flickering brightness. He began with a cartoon, a full-scale preparatory drawing used to plan a large painting. Critics in Rome received it favourably. The version that survives took another ten years and was completed in 1806. Thirteen years separate the first drawing from the final brushstroke.

# Sappho and Alcaeus: Audio Description

**Orientation**

Begin a few steps back from *Sappho and Alcaeus* so the whole wide panel fits in your view. The painting is nearly twice as wide as it is tall, and from a distance you can see how it is built: a single musician on one side, a curved bank of listeners on the other, and the sea beyond them. Then move in close to the white marble seats where the women sit. Letters are carved into the stone, and up close they become readable. That lettering holds the painter's most deliberate change to history.

**The Work**

This is an oil painting on a wooden panel, about 66 by 122 centimetres. It imagines a concert on the Greek island of Lesbos in the late 7th century BC. The performer is Alcaeus of Mytilene, a lyric poet from the island's chief city. He plays the kithara, the large stringed instrument used by professional Greek musicians. Facing him is Sappho, the most celebrated woman poet of the ancient world and his fellow islander. Several of her female friends sit with her.

Sappho leans forward, listening closely. Her arm rests on a cushion, and on that cushion lies a laurel wreath, the traditional prize for a winning performer. It is presumably meant for Alcaeus. The painting gives no sign of whether he will receive it.

The scene illustrates a passage by Hermesianax, a Greek poet whose lines survive only because a later writer quoted them. That writer was Athenaeus, who preserved them in his *Deipnosophistae*, or *The Philosophers' Banquet*, a sprawling collection of dinner-table conversation and quotation. So the painting rests on a fragment of a fragment, a scene reconstructed from a text that itself survives only secondhand.

title: The Laughing Cavalier
output:
# The Laughing Cavalier, by Frans Hals

## Orientation

Stand close to *The Laughing Cavalier*, within arm's length of the frame, and look at the man's right sleeve and lace cuff. From here, the embroidery dissolves into long, quick strokes of the brush, which you cannot see from across the room. Then step back and walk slowly from one side of the painting to the other. His eyes stay on you the whole way.

## The Work

A man of twenty-six turns toward you, one hand on his hip, his elbow pushing out at the viewer. We know his age because Frans Hals painted it into the picture. In the top right corner, a small Latin inscription reads *aetatis suae 26, anno 1624*: "in his twenty-sixth year, in the year 1624." He was therefore born in 1597 or 1598.

We do not know his name. Nineteenth-century titles in Dutch, English and French cast him as a soldier, perhaps an officer in the part-time civic militias that the Dutch liked to have painted in large group portraits. Hals painted several of those groups, and so did Rembrandt, the Amsterdam painter whose *Night Watch* of 1642 is the most famous example. But this man could just as easily have been a wealthy civilian. The art historian Pieter Biesboer has suggested he may be Tieleman Roosterman, a Dutch cloth merchant born in 1598, whom Hals portrayed on another occasion.

Whoever he was, he paid for display. His silk costume was gorgeous and very expensive, and Hals arranged the picture to show it off. The low viewpoint and the turning pose, which Hals used in other portraits too, push the embroidered sleeve and the lace cuff toward the front of the picture. Up close, you can see the trick behind the effect. Embroidery that must have taken someone weeks to stitch is rendered in long, rapid brushstrokes. That speed is what makes the portrait feel lively and spontaneous rather than stiff.

title: A Dance to the Music of Time
output:
# A Dance to the Music of Time, by Nicolas Poussin

## Where to Stand

Stand first at arm's length from the left edge of *A Dance to the Music of Time*, level with the stone pillar beside the dancers. From here you can see that its carved head has two faces, one young and one old. From across the room it reads as a plain garden statue. Then step back to the centre of the room and look up into the sky. The dancers' rhythm is repeated by a second procession overhead, moving across the dawn clouds.

## The Work

Four figures hold hands and dance in a ring, facing outward. On the right, Time sits and plays a lyre. He is the winged, naked, grey-bearded old man. Above them, the day is beginning. Aurora, goddess of the dawn, flies ahead of the chariot of Apollo, the sun-god. Apollo holds a ring that stands for the Zodiac, the circle of constellations that marks the passing year. Around him travel the Hours, the goddesses of time's divisions. Down on the ground, the seasons turn. Up in the sky, the hours turn. Time keeps both in step.

title: Madame de Pompadour
output:
# Madame de Pompadour, by François Boucher

Stand close enough to the canvas of *Madame de Pompadour* that the surface itself comes into focus. From there, the oil paint stops reading as a smooth image and shows the hand of the painter who had studied this same face six times before.

## The Work

This is an oil-on-canvas portrait, painted in 1759, of Madame de Pompadour. Oil paint is slow-drying, so a painter can blend and rework a face over many sittings. That suited a portrait that was meant to refine an image rather than record it for the first time.

That refinement is the key to this canvas. It is the last of seven portraits Boucher painted of her. Each earlier version shaped how she was seen, and this one is the final word in that sequence. Whatever Boucher had settled on after six attempts is what hangs in front of you.

## The Artist

François Boucher was a painter of the French Rococo, the light, ornamental style that dominated French interiors and painting in the eighteenth century. By 1759 he had returned to the same sitter again and again. A series of seven portraits of one person is a sustained working relationship, not a single commission.

The painting was first shown at the Château de Versailles, the French royal palace, before it passed to Madame de Pompadour's brother.

## The Reading

Knowing that this is the seventh and final likeness changes what you see. The face is not a first impression. It is the version that an artist who knew her well chose to leave as his last account of her.

title: Officer and Laughing Girl
output:
# Officer and Laughing Girl: Audio Description

**Orientation**

Stand directly in front of *Officer and Laughing Girl*, about three paces back, with your eyes level with the woman's face. From here the officer's dark back fills the lower left like a shadow cast toward you, and the room seems to recede past him to her and to the open window. Then step close to the wall map behind her. Up close you can see that Vermeer painted it as a real object, mounted on linen and hung from wooden rods.

**The Work**

This is an oil painting on canvas, only 50.5 by 46 centimetres, made around 1657 by the Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer. A young woman sits at a table near a window, with light falling from the left across her face. Opposite her, with his back half-turned to us, sits a cavalry officer in a red coat. His black sash marks his rank as an officer. His wide-brimmed hat is made of beaver pelt, which was prized because it resisted rain and snow. Those pelts were imported from the New World, probably from New Netherland, the Dutch-controlled territory in what is now the eastern United States.

The officer is the painting's key compositional choice. Vermeer pushes him into the immediate foreground, large and dark, so that he frames the brighter, smaller woman beyond him. This device is called repoussoir, which means placing an object up front to deepen the space behind it. Caravaggio, the Italian painter, used it often, and Vermeer probably learned it from the work of Caravaggio's imitators. Art historians also believe Vermeer may have used a camera obscura, a darkened box with a lens that projects an image. That would help explain why the officer looms so much larger than the woman, though they sit only a table's width apart.
